title: State Capitals
description: How well do you know where the state capitals are?

rounds.clue: The capital of Alaska can only be reached by boat or plane — no roads connect it to the rest of the state or Canada. It receives over 90 inches of rain per year.
The capital of Hawaii sits on the island of Oahu and is home to Waikiki Beach, Diamond Head, and one of the busiest fishing harbors in the Pacific.
Sitting at exactly one mile above sea level (5,280 feet), this Colorado capital is nicknamed the Mile High City and served as the gateway to the Gold Rush.
Despite being the capital of the most populous US state, this city is not its largest — that honor goes to Los Angeles. It was a key hub during the Gold Rush.
This Texas capital is called the 'Live Music Capital of the World,' hosts SXSW festival annually, and is home to the University of Texas Longhorns.
The capital of New Mexico is the oldest state capital in the US, founded by Spanish colonists in 1610 — over a decade before the Pilgrims landed at Plymouth.
This capital of Arizona has grown from a frontier town in 1867 to the most populous state capital in the US — over 1.6 million people call it home.
Nevada's capital is not Las Vegas — it's this smaller city named after a Spanish explorer, located in the western part of the state near Lake Tahoe.
The capital of Utah was named by Brigham Young and serves as headquarters for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
Oregon's capital sits in the Willamette Valley surrounded by farms that produce a large share of the nation's hazelnuts, grass seed, and Christmas trees.
Washington State's capital is known for its impressive state capitol dome and its proximity to Puget Sound — though it's often confused with the national capital.
Idaho's capital is named after a French word meaning 'wooded' and sits along the Boise River in the high desert foothills.
Montana's capital sits at the base of Mount Helena and was a booming gold rush town in the 1860s before becoming the state seat of government.
Wyoming's capital is nicknamed the 'Magic City of the Plains' and hosts Cheyenne Frontier Days — the world's largest outdoor rodeo.
North Dakota's capital has the tallest capitol building in the US — an 18-story Art Deco skyscraper nicknamed the 'Skyscraper on the Plains.'
South Dakota's capital was named after a Missouri River steamboat and sits in the center of the state — far from the famous Badlands and Black Hills.
Nebraska's capital has the second-tallest state capitol in the US and is home to the iconic 'Sower' statue atop its dome.
Kansas's capital was the end of the famous Chisholm Trail cattle drive in the 1860s and served as a Wild West boomtown before becoming the state seat.
Oklahoma's capital is the only state capital with an active oil well on its grounds — the capitol building itself sits atop an oil field.
Minnesota's capital sits across the Mississippi River from Minneapolis and is called the 'Twin Cities' — its impressive capitol dome is larger than the US Capitol's.
Iowa's capital sits on the Des Moines River and hosts the largest state fair in the US — a 10-day event attracting over a million visitors.
Missouri's capital is a small city on the Missouri River named for Thomas Jefferson — the man who authorized the Louisiana Purchase.
Wisconsin's capital sits on a narrow isthmus between two lakes and is home to the University of Wisconsin — its campus sits right in the heart of the city.
Illinois's capital is a small city in the center of the state — not Chicago. Abraham Lincoln practiced law here for 17 years before becoming president.
Indiana's capital is home to the Indianapolis Motor Speedway — the world's largest sports venue by capacity, hosting the Indy 500 every May.
Ohio's capital was planned from scratch in 1812 to serve as the state seat — it was never a major river town but grew around government and Ohio State University.
Michigan's capital is not Detroit — it's this smaller city further north, chosen as capital in 1847 partly to be more central to the state.
Kentucky's capital sits along the Kentucky River and is famous for its horse farms — Keeneland Race Course is just minutes away.
Tennessee's capital is the country music capital of the world, home to the Grand Ole Opry, and was a major Union stronghold during the Civil War.
Alabama's capital was the first capital of the Confederacy and the site of the historic 1965 Voting Rights marches from Selma to this city.
Mississippi's capital is named after Andrew Jackson and sits in the center of the state — it hosts the International Ballet Competition every four years.
Louisiana's capital has the tallest state capitol building in the US at 34 stories — built by Governor Huey Long, who was later assassinated in its hallway.
Arkansas's capital is on the Arkansas River and was named by French explorers for a small rock formation they spotted from their boats — 'La Petite Roche.'
Georgia's capital is home to the busiest airport in the world, CNN headquarters, and the world's largest aquarium.
Florida's capital was originally a compromise location — it split the difference between Pensacola and St. Augustine, the two largest cities at the time of statehood.
South Carolina's capital sits at the geographic center of the state and houses Fort Jackson — the largest US Army basic combat training facility.
North Carolina's capital has more state government employees per capita than almost any other city in the US — it was founded specifically to be the state seat.
West Virginia's capital sits at the confluence of the Elk and Kanawha Rivers — its golden-domed capitol was designed by the same architect as the Rhode Island statehouse.
Virginia's capital was the capital of the Confederacy during the Civil War and is home to the oldest continuously operating state legislature in the Western Hemisphere.
Maryland's capital on the Severn River is home to the United States Naval Academy — which has graduated more astronauts than any other undergraduate institution.
Delaware's capital is tiny — fewer than 40,000 people — yet the state whose capital it is hosts the legal addresses of more corporations than any other state.
Pennsylvania's capital on the Susquehanna River sits 100 miles west of Philadelphia — it was the site of a near nuclear disaster at Three Mile Island in 1979.
New Jersey's capital on the Delaware River was George Washington's crossing point on Christmas night 1776 — the surprise attack the next morning turned the Revolution.
New York's capital has been the state seat since 1797 — its Empire State Plaza features a performing arts center nicknamed 'The Egg' for its oval shape.
Connecticut's capital is home to the oldest continuously published newspaper in the US — the Hartford Courant, founded in 1764.
Rhode Island's capital is the smallest state capital by land area in the US and was founded by Roger Williams in 1636 after he was banished from Massachusetts.
Massachusetts's capital is the largest city in New England and home to the Freedom Trail — a 2.5-mile walking path linking 16 historic Revolutionary War sites.
Vermont's capital is the smallest state capital by population in the US — fewer than 8,000 people — nestled in the Green Mountains on the Winooski River.
New Hampshire's capital on the Merrimack River was a major textile manufacturing city in the 19th century, powered by the river's falls.
Maine's capital on the Kennebec River is the home of Blaine House — one of the oldest governor's mansions in continuous use in the United States.
